question: Once the new object classifier has selected a word, does the previously fitted EEG color/layout estimator bring the rendered image closer to the actual colors of the viewed photo?
chronology: The original three-person baseline images, sub-04 mixed images and scores were known. The spatial edits and their scores on these menus had not been inspected. The other two participants were already registered for independent object-encoder replication.
inputs: One own-EEG mixed-readout SDXL image per participant and row, four physical trials per photo, plus the same eight support images and their EEG for the predicted word. Use each participant's existing 512-class eight-by-eight spatial predictor, gain and editing strength without refitting. Do not change the object word, donor, support or noise.
generation: Use the existing fit_spatial_photo.render unchanged. Keep the input JPEG, neutral JPEG re-encode, eight-support spatial mean, own-EEG and wrong-EEG corrections. The two legacy arms are generated by the same driver and excluded from this comparison.
evaluation: Primary global endpoint: after converting the original and generated images to 64x64 RGB using BOX and pooling into an 8x8 grid, calculate RMSE averaged over the two opponent color fields R-Y and B-Y. Report all rows and the correctly predicted objects with a distinct donor that shares true object, predicted word and fold. The latter tests photograph-specific information in chroma. Secondary: 64x64 RGB RMSE and grayscale SSIM, with the original fixed transform. Bootstrap the true object, keeping overlapping observations together across people, 10000 draws seed 260556. Report all three individuals and the pool.
decision: Retain a photo-specific color claim only if the pooled matched color error is lower than the neutral re-encode, the eight-support spatial mean, and the exchanged EEG, with a 95% upper bound below zero for all three differences on the strict subset. If it passes, test independent semantic image naming before proposing to change the primary object model. This is an editing experiment on existing generated JPEGs.
